demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could be stressful
avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Feeling 'dirty or contaminated' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another. This appraisal is much more characteristic of interpersonal violence or sexual trauma, and it does not fit well with the rest of this profile, which centers on danger, guilt/humiliation, physical reactivity, and accident-related pain memories.

issues.item: Triggers: Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
issues.explanation: 'Being forced to do something' is a coercion/interpersonal-control trigger that lacks a clear clinical link to the reported trauma of accidentally injuring someone. The other triggers and memory items suggest accident reminders and bodily pain cues; this item pulls toward a different trauma theme and is not supported by the appraisals or memory content.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: Avoidance of military/police uniforms or weapons is not well grounded in the rest of the profile for an accidental-injury trauma. There are no corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal items involving authority figures, weapons, or armed contexts, so this avoidance strategy appears to target a symptom domain absent elsewhere in the report.

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: The threat profile is not well anchored to the indexed trauma. For accidentally causing serious injury to another, the rest of the profile centers on driving/crash reminders, guilt, pain, and sensory trauma memories. By contrast, 'Threat in Delays' and especially 'Door and Lock Checking' suggest a broader vigilance/checking presentation that is difficult to connect to the accident-specific trigger and memory content.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Within the Threat node, the items mix trauma-linked reactivity ('strong physical reactions when reminded') with generalized danger expectancy in ordinary delays and home-security checking. That combination can occur clinically, but here the latter two items are not supported by corresponding triggers, memories, or appraisals, making the node internally and cross-node less coherent.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Door/window checking implies an ongoing interpersonal/home-intrusion danger theme that is not well supported by the trauma type (accidentally causing serious injury to another) or by the rest of the profile, which is otherwise centered on accident reminders, guilt, and vehicle-related distress.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
issues.explanation: 'The world is a dangerous place' is possible after trauma, but here it pulls the formulation toward diffuse external danger rather than the profile's dominant accident-related guilt/shame theme. In combination with door/window checking, it creates a second threat system not well integrated with the other selected items.

vignette:
Elaine Morgan, a 60-year-old American politician, traced the start of her problems to a campaign-season evening two years earlier when she left a tense town hall after a shouting match with protesters outside the venue. She was driving herself home, her neck already tight from hours of turning between aides and reporters, when she entered an intersection and struck another car. The other driver survived but was seriously injured. Elaine remembers fragments rather than a continuous story: the violent jolt through her neck, the sound of yelling, the sickening sight of the other car crumpled at an angle. What has stayed with her is not a coherent narrative she can summon at will, but isolated sensory pieces that still feel immediate.

In the months after the crash, the things that set her off were painfully specific. Raised voices in legislative meetings, demonstrators shouting outside her office, a stab of neck pain after a long day at the capitol, even the sight of cars that had been hit and left on the roadside could make her body react at once. Her chest tightened, her stomach dropped, and she would feel flooded with fear, shame, and dread before she had even fully registered what had caught her attention. At those moments she would also find herself pulled into the crash again: she could hear yelling in her head as if it were happening now, and when the memory broke through she felt pain in her neck in the same place she had felt it that night.

Those reminders did more than frighten her. Each time they appeared, Elaine was thrown back into the meanings she had attached to the accident. Seeing damaged cars or hearing shouting did not just remind her of danger; it revived her certainty that the event happened because of the way she acted, that she had failed to do more to stop it, and that she had been publicly exposed in a way she could never live down. She had come to believe that she was permanently humiliated by the accident, not only as a driver but as a public figure whose mistakes carried consequences for others. The more intensely she reacted, the more convincing these conclusions felt. A surge of panic or guilt in a committee hearing could leave her thinking, with renewed force, that her body was proving the truth of her disgrace.

Her memory of the accident became organized around this same sense of threat and blame. When she tried deliberately to remember what happened in sequence, she often found she could not reach it. Yet when she was upset, the memory returned in involuntary shards-sound first, then impact, then pain. Those fragments seemed to arrive with their own emotional charge, and the physical reactivity that came with them made the event feel unresolved and present. Because the memories came back this way, she was all the more certain she had never done enough in the moment and never would forgive herself. In turn, that self-condemnation seemed to draw the memory closer, as if her mind kept circling the scene in search of some missed chance to have prevented it.

Over time Elaine began structuring her life around not setting any of this off. She avoided driving altogether and refused to ride with staff unless absolutely necessary, often rearranging public appearances or joining by video when others expected her in person. At work she became vigilant about avoiding anything that might be stressful: contentious meetings, loud rallies, difficult press scrums. She also narrowed her life more broadly, keeping away from anything likely to stir strong feeling, pleasant or unpleasant, because even excitement felt risky if it made her body rev up. That emotional constriction made her days flatter and more rigid, but to Elaine it seemed necessary. She believed that if she let herself feel too much, or entered another high-pressure situation, she would be overwhelmed, exposed, and forced back into what she had done.

These strategies brought short-lived relief, but they tightened the problem. The less she drove or rode in cars, the more alien and charged vehicles became; passing a collision scene from the window of a staff SUV could be enough to send her into a spiral of neck pain, auditory recall, and guilt. Avoiding arguments and public events made shouting seem even more intolerable when it did occur, so a raised voice in a caucus room now hit her with disproportionate force. Because she kept turning away from difficult situations and from her own feelings, she never developed a fuller, steadier account of the accident; instead the memory remained patchy, intrusive, and bodily. That patchiness fed her self-blame-if she could not fully remember, she assumed she must have failed in some unforgivable way-and the shame attached to that belief made her retreat further.

By the time she sought treatment, the consequences were visible in both her work and private life. Staff had noticed that she lost focus in briefings whenever tempers rose, and she had begun declining in-person appearances that once defined her career. Divorced and living alone, she spent more evenings at home, carefully managing her environment to avoid distress. What finally brought her in was a recent incident in which protesters shouted outside a municipal event; Elaine froze, felt searing pain in her neck, heard the crash-era yelling in her head, and could not concentrate enough to deliver her remarks. She came to treatment frightened that her world was shrinking around the accident and equally frightened that if she stopped avoiding it, she would be swallowed by guilt and humiliation she already felt she deserved.
